list.listitem: Prevention using decontaminated water and good food hygiene can be very effective. B
Profound diarrhea can develop very quickly and become life threatening. C
Rapid, aggressive rehydration is essential for control of dehydration and recovery. A
Antibiotics can help to decrease the extent of the disease and control symptoms. A

background.definition: An acute, infectious gastrointestinal illness characterized by profuse watery diarrhea, and often vomiting.

list.listitem: The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that 2.8 million cases of cholera occur annually in endemic countries, and that 87,000 cases occur annually in non-endemic countries.
WHO estimates that about 91,000 deaths are attributed to cholera annually.
There were 10 new cases of cholera in North America in 2006, six of which were imported.
Cholera is caused by toxigenic strains of Vibrio cholerae.
Water and food contaminated with human feces greatly increases risk.

It is generally found in settings where there is inadequate access to clean water and sanitation. A systematic review found that low educational attainment (OR 2.6), unimproved water source (OR 3.5), open container water storage (OR 2.0), household contact with cholera (OR 2.9), and consumption of foood outside the home (OR 2.8) were all associated with an increased risk of cholera. Handwashing was protecting (OR 0.29).
A systematic review found an association between cholera incidence and global climate change, mediated by increases in rainfall, temperature, and sea temperature.
It can rarely be imported into countries where it is not endemic through travel.
Enterotoxin producing V. cholerae causes this noninflammatory diarrhea.

The organism adheres to the intestinal wall and produces cholera toxin. The toxin causes an increase in cAMP, which both inhibits sodium absorption and increases secretion of chloride and bicarbonate.
NaCl accumulates in the lumen, and the increased osmolality causes an increase in water secretion into the lumen.
This process leads to diarrhea, dehydration, and acidosis, which can become severe and life threatening if not addressed quickly.
In epidemic areas, drink only water that has been boiled or treated with chlorine or iodine. C
Untreated water and unwashed produce have been identified as cholera risk factors. Chlorination of household water in the households of cholera victims reduces transmission. B
Eat only foods that have been thoroughly cooked and are still hot, or fruit that you have peeled yourself. C

Cholera whole-cell killed vaccines are relatively safe and effective. Oral vaccines have largely replaced injected vaccines, and efficacy is unlikely to last beyond 3 years without a booster. A case control study during an outbreak of cholera in Africa found that the Shanchol vaccine was 87% effective, as did a study in India finding 65% efficacy at 5 years. Another study found 63% efficacy against severe episdoes and that protection was sustained for two years. A

A single, oral dose of PXVX0200 (recombinant Vibrio cholerae) was studied in children and adolescents aged 6–17 years in the U.S. in a phase 4, placebo-controlled, double-blind, multicenter study. PXVX0200 appears safe, immunogenic, and well tolerated in children and adolescents. There was a smilar seroconversion rate as seen in adults given the vaccine. A
A systematic review following a mass vaccination campaign found no association between vaccine receipt and adverse pregnancy outcomes.
Moderate-to-severe diarrhea (MSD) in the first 2 years of life can impair linear growth, and so the growth and development of young children with a history of cholera should be monitored closely. C
Risk is high in developing countries with contaminated water supplies. C
Profuse, watery diarrhea may lead to massive volume loss and shock. C
Rapid dipstick testscan be helpful in the field in epidemic areas. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Variable inflammation, watery or bloody stool, high fever, moderate-severe abdominal pain
Severe inflammation, watery or bloody stool, high fever, moderate-severe abdominal pain
Minimal inflammation, watery stool but possibly some blood, high fever, moderate-severe abdominal pain
Watery stool, can be quickly bloody, severe abdominal pain, mild fever, minimal nausea and vomiting
Mild watery stool, mild-moderate abdominal pain, minimal nausea and vomiting, mild-moderate fever
Moderate-severe nausea and vomiting, rapid onset, moderate-severe watery diarrhea, minimal abdominal pain, minimal fever

Diagnosis.Diagnostic_criteria: WHO Clinical Case Definition: (1) In an area where the disease is not known to be present, a patient aged 5 years or more develops severe dehydration or dies from acute watery diarrhea, or (2) In an area where there is a cholera epidemic, a patient aged 5 years or more develops acute watery diarrhea with or without vomiting.

list.listitem: Incubation period of 12 to 48 hours.
Patient develops profuse gray "rice-water" watery diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and dehydration. Dehydration can quickly become severe, with hypovolemic shock and acidosis.
Fever and cramping, however, are uncommon because of the nature of the toxin. Patients can also complain of muscle cramping and lightheadedness.
Children can have same symptoms as adults but may also develop drowsiness, fever, and convulsions.
Clinical diagnosisin a high prevalence area (Bangladesh) was moderately accurate.

The WHO clinical case definition is 91% sensitivie and 43% specific in an epidemic setting, with PV+ of 73% and PV− of 75%. Where cholera is not known to be present, the sensitivity is lower (63%) but PPV higher (80%).
Stool culture is preferred when available, and there is no need for rapid diagnosis.

Rapid dipstick testing is preferred in developing countries for field testing, especially during outbreaks. A cholera rapid diagnostic test used in Haiti, had an 89% positive predictive value and 91% negative predictive value compared to stool cultures.
Several rapid antigen detection-based dipstick tests exist. The SMART dipstick assay had the highest sensitivity but somewhat lower specificity than other tests (ex. Crystal VC, Cholkit).
However, the SMART dipstick immunoassay was much less sensitive when used in the field.
A clinical decision rule has been developed and validated to diagnosis clinically important dehydration in children.
Full history required, especially travel history and specific locations.
Physical examination findings vary depending on the amount of volume lost. Common findings are dehydration, muscle cramping, and lightheadedness; fever and abdominal cramping are uncommon.
Stool studies and cultures can help identify cholera as the cause.
Early and aggressive volume replacement is the key to successful recovery. Antibiotics can shorten the course of illness.
Rehydration is the mainstay of therapy. A
Single-dose tetracycline or doxycycline is used in older children and adults; single-dose azithromycin in younger children is effective. A
Use single-dose tetracycline 1 to 2 g or doxycycline 300 mg for older children and adults.
Single-dose azithromycin 1 g is a good alternative, especially for younger children.
Single-dose ciprofloxacin 20 mg/kg in children between the ages of 2 and 15 years achieves better clinical outcomes than 12-dose erythromycin but less eradication of disease.
Fluid replacement is the mainstay of therapy. Adults can receive up to 1000 mL/h of oral rehydration solution (ORS). Children can receive ORS of up to 20 mL/kg of body weight per hour.

The quantity of fluids to administer is determined by the amount of volume depletion and fluid losses. The degree of volume depletion can be categorized by WHO criteria: none (<5 percent of body weight), some (5-10 percent), or severe (>10 percent) based on physical findings. The entire estimated fluid deficit should be replaced within four hours of presentation.
ORS with an osmolarity of <270 mOsm/L has similar clinical outcomes compared to ORS solutions >310 mOsm/L, but was associated with a 67% increase in the risk of biochemical hyponatremia.

CDC guidelines recommend calculating the approximate amount of ORS in milliliters for moderate dehydration by multiplying the patient's weight in kilograms by 75. For example, a 20-kg child would require 1500 mL of ORS if moderately dehydrated.

IV fluids may be necessary if oral fluids fail. Ringer's lactate is preferred, but normal saline is acceptable. Infants younger than 1 year receive 30 mL/kg IV in 1 hour and then 70 mL/kg IV over 5 hours. Those older than 1 year receive 30 mL/kg IV in 30 minutes and then 70 mL/kg IV in 2.5 hours.
Reassess the patient every 1 to 2 hours and increase the rate if no response is seen.
If using IV, give ORS at approx 5 mL/kg per hour as soon as the patient can drink.
Caution is advised with reduced osmolarity solution versus standard WHO ORS because of possible hyponatremia.
Numerous studies have shown that zinc supplementation (10-20 mg per day until cessation of diarrhea) significantly reduces the severity and duration of diarrhea in children less than 5 years of age.
Approximately 75% of patients exposed to cholera will have no symptoms. C
Of those who develop symptoms, 80% will have a mild-moderate case. C
The case fatality rate for developed countries is less than 1%. C
Case fatality rates in endemic areas can be approximately 5%. C
Untreated case fatality rates can approach 50%. C
